messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Seventy-year-old Juan Hernandez had been a welder for most of his life, but it was during his time in the Latin American military that he experienced the traumatic events that continue to shape his life today. He was captured by enemy forces and subjected to torture, including being held captive with no means of escape and being threatened with violence at every turn. Even now, when Juan hears a gunshot noise on TV or sees someone trapped in a situation with no options, he is instantly transported back to that place of helplessness. When these triggers occur, Juan becomes detached from his memories, as if observing himself from afar. He also becomes overly compliant, fawning over those around him in an attempt to avoid any conflict. It's as if he believes that by becoming invisible and agreeable, he can prevent anyone from noticing him or posing a threat. These coping mechanisms have become deeply ingrained, and Juan finds himself employing them even when there is no apparent danger. But the memories themselves are still raw and unprocessed. When Juan tries to recall what happened during his captivity, he becomes enraged - not just at those who perpetrated the violence but also at himself for not doing more to stop it. The memory feels like it's happening all over again, rather than something that occurred decades ago. He can't explain clearly what took place, and when he tries, he gets stuck on certain details and loses his train of thought. Juan is consumed by negative appraisals - a deep-seated fear that harm lurks around every corner, waiting to strike. He believes that if only he had acted differently during the torture, the outcome might have been different. This self-blame has led him to become increasingly withdrawn, avoiding social situations and public places for fear of encountering triggers. As Juan navigates his daily life as a widower, these negative appraisals feed back into his triggers. When he sees someone trapped or threatened in some way - even on TV - it reinforces his own fears of harm and helps him become more vigilant, always on the lookout for potential dangers. And when those memories do surface, they are like a siren call to all the coping mechanisms he's developed over the years. One day, while working as a welder in a small shop, Juan heard the sound of gunfire from a nearby construction site. It was just a celebratory shot for a completed project, but for Juan, it was enough to send him spiraling back into his memories. He became detached and distant, struggling to complete his work that day. The episode shook him so deeply that he finally realized he needed help to break free from the cycle of triggers, maladaptive strategies, and negative appraisals that had defined his life for far too long. It was this realization - coupled with a desperate hope to learn how to silence the memories and re-engage with the world around him - that brought Juan to seek professional help. He's hoping that by confronting these demons head-on, he can finally find some measure of peace in his twilight years.
